analysis.one_liner: Bars enforcement of contracts that silence victims of childhood sexual abuse.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no action since its September 2026 introduction, and only four House Republicans have signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop courts from enforcing contract clauses that prohibit someone from disclosing sexual abuse or the grooming of a minor, based on the bill's title. In practice, that targets the confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements that keep abuse victims from speaking publicly about what happened to them and who was responsible. The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of childhood sexual abuse who signed settlement agreements containing secrecy clauses, and people who have not yet been abused but would be protected because abusers and the institutions around them could no longer rely on contracts to keep victims quiet. The public also gains when abuse and grooming can no longer be hidden behind a signed agreement.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would prohibit the enforcement of contractual clauses that restrict disclosure of sexual abuse and grooming of a minor, meaning a victim could speak publicly about the abuse without the agreement being used against them in court [S1].

analysis.who_pays: The people and institutions that have used confidentiality clauses in settlements to keep abuse hidden — businesses, organizations, and individuals who paid victims to stay silent — would lose their ability to enforce those clauses, and would face public exposure of abuse they had buried. Settlements could also become harder to reach, since a party accused of abuse could no longer guarantee secrecy in exchange for money.

drawbacks.text: Removing confidentiality could make abuse settlements harder to reach, because an accused party may be less willing to pay compensation if it knows the victim can immediately speak publicly; some victims also prefer privacy, and a blanket ban takes that choice away from them [S1].

The bill is titled with the phrase 'and for other purposes,' and the full text is not available in the provided materials, so the bill's complete scope — including exactly which agreements are covered and what 'grooming' covers — cannot be confirmed from the record given here [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is a real gain for abuse survivors: a confidentiality clause would no longer be a legally enforceable gag order. The strongest honest objection is that secrecy is sometimes the price of a settlement at all, so victims whose main need is compensation rather than publicity could end up worse off, and victims who want privacy lose the option of a confidential resolution. The design of those trade-offs cannot be fully judged because the complete text was not provided.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee in mid-September 2026, and the committee has not taken it up; with the session ending in early January 2027, it is running out of time.

narrative.text: Rep. James Comer (R-KY) introduced the bill on September 15, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S3].
The complete action history shows no action after the referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded [S3].
Four House Republicans are listed as cosponsors; no Democrats are on the cosponsor list [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained from the outcome so far: the secrecy clauses the bill targets remain enforceable, and abuse survivors bound by them remain bound, at least while the bill sits without committee action. The public remains unable to hear disclosures that this bill would have protected.

for.name: James Comer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only listed sponsor.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: The committee received the referral on September 15, 2026, and the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled since.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is entirely Republican — Comer plus four of his 222 Republican colleagues — with no Democrats on the cosponsor list, and no votes have occurred that would show how the parties line up [S2].

industries.industry: Institutions that settle abuse claims (employers, schools, youth organizations, religious bodies, entertainment and other businesses)
industries.note: These parties rely on confidentiality clauses in settlement agreements to keep allegations of sexual abuse and grooming of minors out of public view. The bill would make those clauses unenforceable, ending their ability to pay for silence, which is exactly what would let the public learn who abused children and which institutions covered it up [S1].

analysis.trajectory: With only about three and a half months left in the session, no committee action since referral, and just four cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or a floor vote and will most likely die in committee at the end of the Congress.
